- If sentiment is negative in the recent history (especially >1 day), model tends to overcorrect upward — reduce forecast slope or add downward bias.
- When model shows steady upward trend (e.g., +0.1–0.3 per day) and true outcome drops sharply, model is over-optimistic — cap forecast growth or introduce early reversal signal.
- If true outcome has a sharp downward spike (e.g., >5% drop from prior day), model often fails to recognize it — adjust forecast to reflect immediate volatility or add lagged negative sentiment weight.
- Model frequently underestimates the magnitude of true price drops after a spike — apply a “reversion penalty” to forecast if sentiment is neutral or slightly positive.
- If sentiment history shows multiple small positive signals (e.g., 0.2–0.3), model tends to overreact — dampen forecast momentum or reduce slope after 2–3 consecutive positive sentiment days.
- For 30-day horizon, model often overestimates mean reversion — if true outcome shows strong downward trend, reduce forecast by 0.5–1.0 units per 5-day window to align with observed drift.
- If sentiment is neutral or negative for 3+ days, model tends to forecast a “recovery” — suppress upward bias and add a 0.1–0.3 downward drift to forecast unless sentiment turns positive.
